Le 20 septembre dernier, des manifestati: On September 20, demonstrations for and against gender education in schools led to a clash in the streets of Montréal.
Puis, du 7 au 25 octobre, la ville est d: Then, from October 7 to 25, the city became the setting for some fifty hateful acts linked to the war in Gaza. Unfortunate events, such as the attack on a Montréal woman because of her support for the Palestinian cause and the Molotov cocktail attack on a Jewish centre, reminded us of the relentless rise in violence.
Face à cette violence et à la polarisati: In the face of this violence and the polarization of public debate, La Converse consulted two specialists, one in radicalization and the other in intercultural mediation.
Ces deux professionnels partagent une co: Both professionals share a conviction: dialogue remains the essential remedy for emerging from this toxic climate.
Louis Audet-Gosselin est le directeur sc: Louis Audet-Gosselin is the scientific and strategic director of the Centre for the Prevention of Radicalization Leading to Violence (CPRMV). The organization is a research centre that also offers educational services on radicalization, as well as support and psychological intervention, to the people of Montréal and Quebec.
« Lorsque nous parlons de radicalisation: “When we talk about radicalization, we are mainly referring to a very strong identification with an exclusive group that sees itself as being in violent opposition to other groups in society,” the director begins.
« Cela signifie qu’on ne peut plus enten: “It means you can no longer hear other people’s points of view, which leads to a form of dehumanization of the other and to the legitimization of violence, often at the expense of democratic principles.” According to him, this phenomenon can occur in any political group.
Plusieurs facteurs de vulnérabilité pous: Several vulnerability factors push certain individuals, marked by a sense of marginalization and social exclusion, down the path of radicalization.
« Que ce soit une réalité objective ou u: “Whether it’s an objective reality or a biased perception, many people feel excluded and targeted, believing they don’t have the right to express controversial opinions, to doubt, or even to voice criticism without being stigmatized.”
Il évoque l’exemple d’adolescents tombés: He cites the example of teenagers who have fallen under the sway of the masculinist influencer Andrew Tate. “These boys turn to misogyny because they feel excluded and socially devalued.”
Il explique également que le sentiment d: He also explains that the feeling of marginalization reinforces the perception of injustice, of a “double standard.”
« Il y a une surreprésentation des indiv: “People who live mainly in the virtual world are overrepresented among those who commit violent acts in the name of an ideology. There is a fairly extreme disconnect from real society.”
Le chercheur note que la majorité des pe: The researcher notes that most people who become radicalized often have a relatively homogeneous, not very diverse social circle. “Online, we’re no longer necessarily in a society where we have to deal with all kinds of people, including those who annoy us, or even those we like in spite of our differences, for one reason or another. All of that disappears. It’s becoming more and more common to shut ourselves into bubbles where people share our opinions.”
L’écran crée également une distance par: The screen also creates distance from face-to-face conversations, where humanizing the other person is more likely. “In the virtual world, it’s easier to dehumanize those who don’t share our opinions – which fosters polarization and violence.”
Les réseaux sociaux jouent également un: Social media also plays a significant role in this. “The speed at which information spreads on these platforms fuels polarization. Instant reactions leave no time to verify information or consider different perspectives, which leads to a rapid escalation of tensions. And algorithms can also push users toward increasingly extreme content.”

« Dans les délibérations publiques, les: “In public deliberations, debates quickly become polarized around radical solutions or ones clearly opposed to the other side, pushing aside every position that isn’t at the extremes. This tendency to see any difference as opposition stifles nuance and reinforces common cognitive biases.”
Dans la société actuelle, « on est vraim: In today’s society, “we are truly in urgent need of spaces for dialogue,” he says.
Le directeur scientifique et stratégique: The scientific and strategic director believes that in Quebec, there is indeed a tendency to set up dialogues hastily, often in reaction to crisis situations. “Especially in schools, where teachers are overwhelmed. Dialogue isn’t the priority when you consider the level of stress they face.”
Le même constat vaut pour les organismes: The same goes for community organizations: “They’re underfunded,” says D<sup>r</sup> Audet-Gosselin.
« Publiquement, il n’y a plus d’espace p: “Publicly, there’s no longer any room to express doubts without being demonized. This lack of dialogue means that when people look for a place to speak up, they end up running into extremist groups.”
« La majorité des gens ne sont probablem: “Most people probably aren’t as clear-cut in their initial point of view. But there are real cores of people who will exploit crises for extremist ends, because they have hateful intentions. These organized groups are ready to supply ready-made answers and to organize demonstrations to bring all these people together.”
Puis, le dialogue a un grand objectif :: Dialogue, then, has one big goal: to humanize. “So you have to approach it with kindness, without judgment and with the intention of understanding – not of convincing.”
Il donne par ailleurs comme conseil aux: He also advises people who witness a radicalization process to visit the CPRMV’s <l1>website</l1> and use the resources the organization offers.
« On ne peut aider que ceux qui sont ouv: “We can only help those who are open to receiving help. That’s why the role of witnesses is crucial. Pour savoir comment parvenir à établir u: To learn how to establish a dialogue, we consulted Michèle Vatz Laaroussi, a professor in the School of Social Work at Université de Sherbrooke. She played a key role in designing and launching the master’s program in intercultural mediation at the university.
Dans le <em>Guide d’accompagnement pour: In the Guide d’accompagnement pour une recherche action-médiation, the researcher and her colleagues emphasize that “dialogue is not a adversarial debate, a one-way speech, an argument or a quest for truth.”
« Il s’agit plutôt d’un échange de parol: “It is rather an exchange of words, ideas and convictions, rooted in recognition of the other person and their difference. It is a co-creation.”
L’initiative du dialogue survient à la s: The initiative for dialogue arises from the realization that polarization harms everyone – people on one side as well as the other, or, more simply, individuals within society.
« Le dialogue n’est généralement envisag: “Dialogue is generally only possible within small groups, especially in times of conflict and high tension,” says the social worker. She cites demonstrations and counter-demonstrations as examples of situations that are not conducive to dialogue.
« Dans les moments où nous sommes en con: “When we’re in confrontation, we’re rarely able to give up our own position and step out of our own emotions to listen to the other person. However, it’s possible to organize dialogues after a demonstration, or even before, in order to limit the damage as much as possible during these events.”
« Les personnes qu’on approche pour part: “The people we approach to take part in dialogue are generally those who are not strongly polarized and who are closer to the centre,” she explains. “These individuals play a major role, because after the dialogue, they can explore other positions and facilitate discussions with their peers within their own group.”
« Qu’il s’agisse d’alliés, d’organisatio: “Whether they are allies, facilitating organizations or professional mediators, the presence of a third party is crucial, because it helps avoid falling into debate and makes real dialogue possible,” adds M<sup>s</sup> Vatz Laaroussi.
« Ça peut sembler évident, mais les médi: “It may seem obvious, but mediators must remain impartial while ensuring that every individual is respected. They are guides for the participants and steer them toward nonviolent communication,” she insists.
<strong>Un climat convivial et un enviro: A friendly atmosphere and a safe environment
« La création d’une atmosphère convivial: “Creating a friendly atmosphere is essential.” To encourage the informal development of individual connections, Professor Vatz Laaroussi recommends “sharing a meal or a snack” or “having each group bring its own contribution.” Artistic expression is also a good way.
« Un environnement sécuritaire se caract: “A safe environment is one that recognizes the diversity of society, honouring each individual in the richness of their identity.” It also requires putting in place rules that promote nonviolent communication. “For example, you have to speak from the ‘I’ rather than speaking on behalf of the other party. That’s essential to keep communication respectful, sincere and deep.”
Puis, « [les médiateurs] doivent être… a: Then, “[mediators] must be… attentive to remarks that may be insulting, racist or hurtful so they can address them quickly and not let power relations and inequalities be reproduced during the mediation.”
« Il faut penser à un lieu de rencontre,: “You have to think about a meeting place that’s equidistant for everyone and that accommodates participants in terms of accessibility.”
Il ne suffit pas de réunir des parties q: It is not enough to bring opposing parties together in a dialogue. The professor explains that a third party must first meet these groups separately, as preparation. “This is what we call pre-mediation.”
Elle insiste sur l’importancede cette ét: She stresses the importance of this step, because it allows the members of each group to speak completely freely with people who share their ideology.
« Cela crée un espace de sécurité cultur: “It creates a space of cultural safety, where everyone feels at ease within their own group. It allows participants to express themselves without restraint, sometimes forcefully, even violently, but in a climate of mutual trust, without judgment,” she adds.
Au cours de cette étape, le conflit peut: During this stage, the conflict can be put on the table and examined from other angles.
Lors de la médiation « Les féminismes en: During the mediation “Les féminismes en dialogue”*, the organizers prepared several exercises to move toward dialogue. One of them focuses on self-definition, a process that, for many, is “a first reflection on the question ‘Who are we?’, without being categorized by others.”
L’exercice « J<em>e</em> nous vois, je l: The exercise “I see us, I see them, they [iels] see me,” for its part, invites each person to express their impressions of their own group as well as of a group they perceive as distant. This reflection aims to address tensions and encourages participants to share their experiences and their prejudices.

Le rôle d’une tierce partie est d’aider: The role of a third party is to help participants deconstruct prejudices and their origins, while humanizing both sides. “What causes conflict, most often, is prejudice, incomprehension, mutual ignorance and a lot of misunderstandings,” the professor points out. “Before entering into dialogue and meeting the other side, all of that has to be acknowledged.”
Le facteur temps revêt aussi une grande: Time is also a major factor in the success of a dialogue. “You have to allow the necessary time for each stage, both the pre-mediation and the dialogue meeting.”
Durant la médiation « Les féminismes en: During the mediation “Les féminismes en dialogue,” the pre-mediation session lasted from two and a half to three hours. The dialogue meetings then took place over two days, with a schedule that made it possible to approach the conflict in several ways.
« Il faut du temps pour que les changeme: “It takes time for change to happen, to come to want a dialogue, to cultivate open-mindedness and to question yourself. Rather than imposing a rigid deadline on yourself, it makes more sense to adopt a personal pace and adapt to that of the person you’re in dialogue with.”
<strong>Personne ne détient la vérité, m: No one holds the truth, only a truth
Selon la professeure, pour amorcer un di: According to the professor, to begin a dialogue, you first need to decentre yourself. “First of all, we have to recognize that we perceive the world through glasses, whether they’re cultural, social, economic or something else,” she explains. “We don’t have the absolute truth; at best, we have a part of our truth.”
Cette décentration ne se fera pas d’un c: This decentring won’t happen all at once, but gradually. As a first step toward openness, you can begin the mediation by engaging with cultural and artistic works. “Whether it’s reading a novel, watching a film or listening to music, whatever kind of art resonates with you, it’s a way of broadening your horizons by exploring other people’s emotional dimensions.”
« Le fait que nous soyons prêt à dialogu: “Just because we’re ready to engage in dialogue doesn’t mean the other person is too. If we rush in too early, it won’t work, and it will only increase our mutual frustration,” she explains.
Il est essentiel d’attendre que l’autre: It is essential to wait for the other person to join us, because we don’t all move at the same pace. “People do eventually find each other, but it takes time. Time to find the right words, to avoid causing hurt.”
L’élément clé, ici, est de partager ses: The key element here is sharing emotions, because that is how empathy is born. It means moving away from the approach of persuasion at all costs and instead leading people to not judge, to be vulnerable.
« Cela signifie qu’on ne cherche pas à b: “It means we’re not trying to hurt the other person; we also don’t want to be hurt. The idea is to create a situation where mutual respect allows us to speak sincerely and to understand what the other person feels or says.”
À l’aide des alliés, on peut vraiment dé: With the help of allies, we can truly move beyond judgment to address the underlying emotions. “What scares us? What troubles us? What hurts us? What concerns us? It’s by exploring these emotional aspects that we can hope to create a real dialogue and understand everyone’s perspectives.”
M<sup>me</sup> Vatz Laaroussi propose d’: M<sup>s</sup> Vatz Laaroussi also proposes an artistic expression exercise that uses the form of correspondence, in which each person is invited to write a letter to someone in the opposing group.
Dans le <em>Guide d’accompagnement pour: In the Guide d’accompagnement pour une recherche action-médiation, she lays out an outline for this type of letter: “1. Introduce yourself; 2. Explain how you feel incomprehension, tension or conflict in the relationship; 3. Express your emotions about these tensions and conflicts; 4. Conclude by suggesting possible strategies to bring the parties closer together.”
« L’écriture apporte un changement signi: “Writing brings a significant change to how we express ourselves, compared with oral communication. Emotions, especially anger, are expressed differently, and reflecting on the words used in writing takes centre stage,” she explains.
L’objectif est de réaliser que « nous pa: The goal is to realize that “we share the same emotions, so that we can create empathy.”
« L’empathie ne consiste pas à dire “J’a: “Empathy doesn’t mean saying ‘I like the other person’ or ‘The other person is right on every point,’ but recognizing that I can understand the other person’s emotions.”
« C’est évident qu’on ne peut pas toujou: “Obviously, we can’t always get to empathy. However, even in its absence, expressing emotions can at least lead to listening and to respect for what the other person has to say.”
<strong>Nous sommes capables d’autre cho: We are capable of more than violence
Dans le contexte politique actuel, qui e: In today’s political context, which is increasingly polarized and dark, Michèle Vatz Laaroussi, like Louis Audet-Gosselin, is convinced that “we must keep believing in the possibility of dialogue.” “It is essential to keep faith in our ability to choose alternatives to destruction, aggression and violence,” she adds.
En songeant à la situation mondiale qui: Reflecting on the current global situation, the professor notes: “We live in a world where violence seems to be spreading, where conflicts are increasing. So this is the right time to promote and initiate dialogues. We shouldn’t be afraid to want to change things, even if it’s only on a small scale.”
